overview: Both copy genetic information using a DNA template, but one duplicates the whole genome and the other reads a gene into RNA.
genZNote: Replication makes a backup of the whole book. Transcription just photocopies one chapter you actually need right now.

aspects.label: Purpose
aspects.valueA: Duplicates the entire DNA molecule before cell division so each daughter cell gets a full genome.
aspects.valueB: Copies a specific gene into RNA so its information can be used to make a protein.

aspects.label: Product
aspects.valueB: A single-stranded RNA molecule (mRNA, tRNA, or rRNA).

aspects.label: Template Used
aspects.valueA: Both strands of the DNA act as templates simultaneously.
aspects.valueB: Only the template (antisense) strand of one gene is read.

aspects.label: Timing in Cell Cycle
aspects.valueA: Occurs once per cell cycle, during S phase.
aspects.valueB: Occurs continuously, whenever a gene needs to be expressed.

aspects.label: Base Pairing Rule
aspects.valueA: A-T and G-C, using free deoxyribonucleotides.
aspects.valueB: A-U (not A-T) and G-C, using free ribonucleotides.

aspects.label: Fidelity / Proofreading
aspects.valueA: Very high fidelity with proofreading (3'-5' exonuclease activity).
aspects.valueB: Lower fidelity; errors are less costly since RNA is short-lived.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Replication is semi-conservative; transcription is not conservative at all — the DNA template is reused, not consumed.
overlay.memoryTrick: Replication: DNA to DNA. Transcription: DNA to RNA.
overlay.commonMisconception: Students often think transcription copies the whole gene into DNA — it copies one strand of one gene into RNA.
